h.en: The Four Principles: Abstraction, Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism

body.en:
Object-Oriented Programming models software the way humans see the world - as objects with data and behaviour. Four principles support everything built with it:

  • Abstraction - show only what the user needs, hide the rest. You press an ATM's "Withdraw" button and never see its inner code. In Java: abstract classes and interfaces (Unit 3).
  • Encapsulation - keep data and the methods that guard it together in one safe box (the class), making fields private and offering public methods. A capsule protects its medicine the same way.
  • Inheritance - a new class reuses an existing class and only adds or changes what is special: class Car extends class Vehicle.
  • Polymorphism (many forms) - the same name doing different work: add(2,3), add(2,3,4) and add(2.5,7.5) all "add" in their own way.

These four are the favourite definition question of Unit 2 - learn one real-world example for each.

• A class is a user-defined blueprint: it describes which data (fields) and which actions (methods) its objects will have.
  • An object is a real instance created with new: Student s1 = new Student(); - the class name is the type, new reserves memory in the heap.
  • Fields (int roll; String name;) hold the state of each object separately; the dot operator reaches members: s1.roll, s1.display().
  • A method called on an object works with that object's own fields - display() of s1 prints s1's data.

Run the Student program and see how two objects keep separate values even though the code is written once.

• A constructor is a special member that initializes a freshly created object. Rules: same name as the class, no return type (not even void), called automatically by new.
  • Default constructor: no parameters - gives fixed starting values. If you write NO constructor at all, Java quietly supplies an empty default one.
  • Parameterized constructor: receives values used to set up the object differently each time.
  • Constructor overloading: several constructors with different parameter lists; the compiler selects by the new call's arguments.
  • Constructors are not methods (they cannot be called like obj.Book()) and are not inherited.

• this is a reference to the current object - the one on which the method or constructor is running.
  • Use 1 - shadowing: when a parameter has the same name as a field, this.name = name; assigns the parameter into the field.
  • Use 2 - constructor chaining: this(...) as the first statement of a constructor calls another constructor of the same class, so shared setup is written once.
  • Use 3 - current object as a value: return this; or passing this as an argument.

• static members belong to the class, not to any object: there is exactly ONE copy, created when the class is loaded.
  • Static variable - shared by all objects; the classic counter in the live program.
  • Static method - called with the class name (Counter.report()), receives no this, and can directly touch only static members. main() is static for this reason.
  • Static block - runs once when the class is loaded, before main(); used for one-time setup.
  • A static nested class is a helper class attached to an outer class without needing an outer object (Unit 5 uses it in lambdas' cousins).

Access modifiers decide who may use a class member:

  • private - only inside the same class. Hiding fields as private is the heart of encapsulation.
  • default (no keyword written) - visible everywhere in the same package.
  • protected - package + subclasses in any package (needed with inheritance, Unit 3).
  • public - visible from anywhere.
  • Order from most open to most restricted: public > protected > default > private.
  • Good practice: fields private, behaviour public - outsiders change data only through checked methods (deposit() rejects negative amounts).

• Definition: returnType name(parameters) { body } - e.g. int add(int x, int y) { return x + y; }.
  • Calling: run the method by its name with matching arguments: int s = add(7, 5);. Values flow into parameters; return sends exactly one value back.
  • void methods return nothing - they just do work.
  • Method overloading: the same name with different parameter lists (number or type). The compiler picks the match at compile time - this is compile-time (static) polymorphism. Return type alone cannot overload.

h.en: The String Class and Common Methods

body.en:
• String is a class; texts are objects created from literals: String s = "GTU Diploma";.
  • Strings are immutable - every change creates a new string; ten edits create ten objects (for heavy editing use StringBuilder).
  • Top methods for the exam: length(), charAt(i), substring(be), toUpperCase(), toLowerCase(), indexOf(), contains(), trim(), replace(), equals(), concat(), split(), join().
  • Positions are 0-based; substring's end index is excluded.
  • Compare text with equals(), NEVER with == (that compares references and works only accidentally when both literals share one object).

• Java is object oriented, but primitives are not objects. Every primitive has an object twin - a wrapper class: Byte, Short, Integer, Long, Float, Double, Character, Boolean.
  • Why wrap? Collections (Unit 4) store only objects; wrappers also carry helpers: Integer.parseInt(), MAX_VALUE, toBinaryString().
  • Autoboxing - automatic primitive -> wrapper: Integer o = 42;. Unboxing - automatic wrapper -> primitive: int m = o;. Before Java 5 this was written by hand with valueOf() / intValue().
  • Wrapper objects can be null, so unboxing a null throws an exception (Unit 4).

h.en: Scanner Class and Command Line Arguments

body.en:
• Scanner (java.util) reads typed input: attach it to System.in once, then use nextLine() for whole lines, next() for one token, nextInt(), nextDouble() for numbers.
  • The ENTER trap: numeric reads leave the pressed Enter in the queue, so a following nextLine() returns empty. Cure: one extra sc.nextLine() right after the number.
  • Command line arguments - strings given after the run command (java Main 15 27) arrive in String[] args: no waiting, perfect for fixed settings; convert with Integer.parseInt().

h.en: Garbage Collection and the finalize() Method

body.en:
• Java frees memory automatically: the garbage collector removes objects that no reference can reach anymore. There is no free() / delete keyword like in C++.
  • An object becomes garbage when its references are gone: it = null;, or the variable goes out of scope.
  • System.gc() only requests a collection - the JVM decides when and in which order; you can never force it.
  • finalize() is invoked by the JVM on an object just before destruction - a last chance to release external resources. It is deprecated in modern Java in favour of try-with-resources (Unit 5), but you must know it for the syllabus.

title.en: A Student class: fields, methods, object creation

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
1 : Asha
2 : Bhavesh

expl.en:
Practical 4. A class is a blueprint; an object is a real copy made from it with new.

  • Fields (roll, name) store data; methods (setData, display) define behaviour.
  • Two objects hold independent values: setting s2 does not change s1.
  • Methods are called on an object with a dot: s1.display();.

title.en: Methods: parameters, return values and calling

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
sum = 12
Hi Sunil
avg = 80.0

expl.en:
• A method definition has: return type, name, parameter list, body.
  • Method calling copies values into the parameters; return sends one value back to the caller.
  • void methods (greet) perform an action but return nothing.
  • Methods inside the same class as main() are called plain (add(7, 5)) because both are static.

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
Java Rs. 0.0
OOP in Java Rs. 299.0

expl.en:
Practical 5(a). A constructor initializes the new object. It has the same name as the class and no return type (not even void).

  • The default constructor takes no arguments; the parameterized constructor receives values.
  • this distinguishes the field (this.title) from the parameter (title) when both have the same name.
  • Which constructor runs is decided by the argument list of new.

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
Guest -> 0.0
Riya -> 500.0
Amit -> 5000.0

expl.en:
• Constructor overloading = several constructors with different parameter lists in one class.
  • The compiler picks the one whose signature matches the new call.
  • Gives users flexible ways to create objects with more or less initial data.

title.en: The 'this' keyword: shadowing and constructor chaining

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
Note 12 Rs. 14999.0
Galaxy Rs. 21249.0
Galaxy Rs. 21249.0

expl.en:
• this.field solves shadowing: parameter names normally hide the fields.
  • this(args) calls another constructor of the same class - chaining avoids duplicate code (must be the first statement).
  • this as a value refers to the current object: m1.bigger(m2) returns this (m1) or o (m2), and show() runs on the result.

title.en: The 'static' keyword: variable, method and block

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
class loading...
c.id = 3
total = 3
3

expl.en:
Practical 5(b).

  • A static variable belongs to the class, not to objects: all objects share one total, while each has its own id.
  • A static block runs once when the class is loaded - before main() starts.
  • A static method can be called with the class name (Counter.report()) and can touch only static members directly.
  • Static classes (nested) group related helper classes - seen again in Unit 5.

title.en: Access modifiers with getters and setters

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
owner = Sunil
bank = SBI
balance = 1200.0

expl.en:
• private - only inside the same class; default (no keyword) - anywhere in the same package; protected - package + subclasses (Unit 3); public - everywhere.
  • Hiding bal and giving public getters/setters is encapsulation: the check if (amt > 0) prevents nonsense changes.
  • Try uncommenting ac.bal = 99999; - the compiler itself stops you.

Practical 6.

  • Method overloading: several methods share one name but differ in the number or type of parameters - the compiler chooses by matching the call.
  • Changing only the return type is NOT enough; the parameter list must differ.
  • This is compile-time (static) polymorphism - the decision is made at compile time.

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
11
D
Diploma
GTU
GTU DIPLOMA
gtu diploma
4
true
true
hi
GTU Diploma 2026
GTU diploma
true
true

expl.en:
Practical 7. String is immutable: every method returns a NEW string, s itself never changes.

  • substring(4) = from index 4 to the end; substring(0,3) = 0,1,2 (end excluded).
  • indexOf gives the first position, or -1 if absent.
  • equals() compares text; == compares references - two strings with the same text may or may not share memory (here both literals do - see output).

title.en: String joining, splitting and an array of strings

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
0 : red
1 : green
2 : blue
red - green - blue
J A V A 
JAVA

expl.en:
• split(",") breaks a string around the separator and returns a String[] array.
  • String.join(" - ", parts) glues array pieces with a separator.
  • toCharArray() gives the characters as a char[]; new String(ch) builds a string back.
  • These three appear constantly in data-entry and CSV-style programs.

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
42
7.5 A true
154
9.0
2147483647
-2147483648
1010

expl.en:
• Wrapper classes box each primitive into an object: Byte, Short, Integer, Long, Float, Double, Character, Boolean.
  • Objects are needed because collections (Unit 4) store only objects, and wrapper classes carry helpers like parseInt and MAX_VALUE.
  • Integer.parseInt("153") converts text entered by a user into a real number - without it "153" + 1 would be "1531".

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
Enter name: Enter marks (int): Enter CGPA: name: Sunil Patel
box marks=452
marks int = 453
box CGPA=8.25
CGPA unbox=8.25

expl.en:
Practical 8.

  • Scanner (java.util) reads user input: nextLine() text, nextInt() whole numbers, nextDouble() decimals - the program waits for you to type.
  • Autoboxing: Java automatically wraps a primitive into its wrapper object (Integer mObj = marks;).
  • Unboxing: the opposite (int m2 = mObj;), done automatically too. Before Java 5 you had to write Integer.valueOf() / intValue() by hand.

Try it live: the output shows what the program printed after reading name = Sunil Patel, marks = 452, CGPA = 8.25.

title.en: Scanner: mixed input and nextLine pitfalls

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
Age: Full name: Single token: age = 19
name = Priya Sharma
token = hello

expl.en:
• nextInt() reads only the number; the ENTER you pressed stays in the queue.
  • The extra sc.nextLine() consumes that leftover ENTER - without it, the following nextLine() would read an empty line and the program would seem to "skip" the name input.
  • next() reads one token (stops at space): "hello extra" gives back only "hello".

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main 15 27
count = 2
0 : 15
1 : 27
sum = 42

expl.en:
• Everything typed after java Main ... lands inside args as strings.
  • This run used java Main 15 27 - see both values and their sum in the output window.
  • Arguments reach the program without any Scanner; parse with Integer.parseInt for numbers.
  • Great for small tools where input stays fixed per run.

title.en: Garbage collection and the finalize() method

programs.out:
$ javac Main.java
$ java Main
collecting pen
collecting book
collecting bag
main ends

expl.en:
• Java's garbage collector (GC) frees memory of objects that have no reference left - exactly like it after it = null;.
  • finalize() is called by the JVM on an object just before it is destroyed - a last chance to clean up (e.g. close a file). Note it is deprecated in modern Java; modern code uses try-with-resources instead (Unit 5).
  • System.gc() only requests collection; the order and timing belong to the JVM, never to you.
  • The output shows each item being collected right after it becomes unreachable.

q.en: What is OOP?

a.en: A way of organising programs around objects that hold data (fields) and behaviour (methods), instead of procedures.

q.en: Name the four principles of OOP.

a.en: Abstraction, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism.

q.en: What is abstraction? Give an example.

a.en: Showing only the necessary features and hiding the details - an ATM user sees buttons, not the dispensing machinery. Done via abstract classes and interfaces.

q.en: What is encapsulation? Give an example.

a.en: Binding data and its guarding methods inside one class, with private fields - like a capsule protecting medicine; BankAcc keeps bal private and checks deposit().

q.en: What is inheritance?

a.en: Creating a new class by reusing an existing class with keyword extends, so common code is written once.

q.en: What is polymorphism?

a.en: "Many forms": the same name doing different work, e.g. overloaded add() methods; runtime version comes via overriding (Unit 3).

q.en: What is a class? What is an object?

a.en: A class is a blueprint (a type) describing fields and methods; an object is a real instance of it living in heap memory, created with new.

q.en: Difference between fields and local variables?

a.en: Fields belong to an object and live as long as it; local variables exist only inside their method or block.

q.en: How do you access members of an object?

a.en: With the dot operator: s1.roll and s1.display().

q.en: What is a constructor?

a.en: A special member that runs automatically at new to initialize the object; it has the class name and no return type.

q.en: What is a default constructor?

a.en: A constructor with no parameters; if a class has none, Java adds an empty one silently.

q.en: What is a parameterized constructor?

a.en: A constructor that receives values, e.g. new Book("Java", 299) initializes title and price in one step.

q.en: What is constructor overloading?

a.en: Several constructors with different parameter lists in one class; the compiler matches the new call.

q.en: Can a constructor have a return type or be called on an object?

a.en: No - a return type (even void) would turn it into an ordinary method, and obj.Book() is illegal.

q.en: Differentiate constructor and method.

a.en: Class name vs any name; no return type vs mandatory one; runs at new vs when called; not inherited vs inheritable.

q.en: What is this keyword?

a.en: A reference to the current object - used to separate fields from same-named parameters, to chain constructors with this(), and to return the current object.

q.en: Where must this() be written?

a.en: As the very first statement of a constructor.

q.en: What is static variable?

a.en: A class-level variable with a single copy shared by all objects, loaded once when the class loads.

q.en: What is static method?

a.en: A method callable with the class name; it has no this and can directly use only static members.

q.en: Why is main() static?

a.en: The JVM must start the program without creating any object first.

q.en: What is a static block and when does it run?

a.en: A block that runs once when the class is loaded, before main().

q.en: List the four access modifiers in restrictiveness order.

a.en: private < default < protected < public (private most restricted).

q.en: Difference between default and protected?

a.en: default is visible inside the same package only; protected also in subclasses outside the package.

q.en: Why keep fields private?

a.en: So outside code cannot put illegal values: changes pass through checked public methods (encapsulation).

q.en: What are getters and setters?

a.en: Public methods that read (getBal) or update (deposit) private fields under control of the class.

q.en: What is method overloading?

a.en: Same method name with different parameter lists in one class; decided at compile time (compile-time polymorphism).

q.en: Is changing only the return type valid overloading?

a.en: No - the parameter list must differ; the return type alone cannot overload.

q.en: What is a String in Java?

a.en: A class; its objects hold immutable character text built from literals like "GTU".

q.en: What does string immutability mean?

a.en: Methods never change the original string - they create and return a new one.

q.en: Give any four String methods with purpose.

a.en: length() size, charAt(i) ith char, substring() part of the text, indexOf() first position.

q.en: s == t vs s.equals(t)?

a.en: == compares references (same object?); equals() compares the actual text - always use equals for strings.

q.en: What does s.substring(0, 3) return for "GTU"?

a.en: GTU - characters 0, 1 and 2; the end index is excluded.

q.en: What do split() and join() do?

a.en: split(",") breaks a string into a String[] around the separator; String.join("-", arr) glues the pieces back.

q.en: What is a wrapper class? Name all eight.

a.en: The object twin of a primitive: Byte, Short, Integer, Long, Float, Double, Character, Boolean.

q.en: What are autoboxing and unboxing?

a.en: Automatic conversions since Java 5: primitive -> wrapper (Integer o = 42) and wrapper -> primitive (int m = o).

q.en: Why are wrapper classes needed?

a.en: Collections store objects only, and wrappers supply parsing helpers like Integer.parseInt().

q.en: What happens on unboxing a null?

a.en: A NullPointerException is thrown - wrapper objects may be null unlike primitives.

q.en: How do you read a whole line and an integer with Scanner?

a.en: new Scanner(System.in); nextLine() reads a line, nextInt() reads an int.

q.en: What is the nextLine() pitfall after nextInt()?

a.en: nextInt() leaves the pressed Enter; the next nextLine() reads it as an empty line. Use one extra nextLine() to consume it.

q.en: What is next() vs nextLine()?

a.en: next() reads one space-separated token; nextLine() reads the whole line.

q.en: What are command line arguments?

a.en: Strings written after the run command: java Main 15 27 -> args = {"15","27"}; converted with parseInt.

q.en: What is garbage collection?

a.en: The automatic freeing of heap memory holding objects that no reference can reach; there is no delete keyword.

q.en: What does System.gc() guarantee?

a.en: Nothing - it only requests collection; the JVM decides the time and order.

q.en: What is finalize()?

a.en: A method the JVM calls on an object just before destroying it (last clean-up); deprecated now - try-with-resources is preferred.

q.en: Why is memory management in Java called automatic?

a.en: Because objects are created with new and destroyed by the garbage collector - the programmer never frees memory by hand.

q.en: Combine: how do encapsulation, getter/setter and private relate in BankAcc?

a.en: bal is private (hidden), deposit() checks amt > 0 (controlled change), getBal() is the only way to read it - that is encapsulation in practice.
